passage:
Dear Uday,
Since you're coming to the family wedding next month, let me tell you what I learnt at Diwali. Within ten minutes, three aunties asked me: job? salary? marriage? One said, "At your age I had a baby." I smiled, went up to the terrace and felt like a failed exam paper.
For a week I was angry. Then I started to see it: they're using a clock from their own time. Graduate at 21, job at 22, married at 24. It isn't my clock, but it isn't cruel either.
So here's what I say now, kindly: "I'm working on it, Aunty. How's your knee?" Short, warm, then a new subject. I don't argue and I don't promise dates.
You'll get the same questions. You don't owe anyone your timeline.
Your didi,
Pallavi

qa.a: "At your age I had a baby."

qa.q: How did Pallavi feel on the terrace?
qa.a: Judged and small, like a failed exam paper.

qa.q: How might the aunties see their own questions?

Within minutes three relatives had found her. Mausi: "Next it's your wedding, na? Twenty-two is the right age." Chachaji: "Lab assistant? What's the salary? Your cousin in Pune gets double." An aunty: "Don't wait too long, beta."

Then she took a breath and said, "When it's right for me, Mausi, you'll be the first to know. And the lab work is exactly what I wanted." She said it gently and didn't argue. Afterwards she came and took the baby from me and held it for a long time.

I'm in my final year of design. I don't have a job offer. I'm not dating anyone.

The first night I snapped at my uncle and felt awful after.
The second night, I tried something else. When he asked, I smiled. "I'll tell you when there's news, Chacha. Tell me about your garden?"
He talked for twenty minutes. I went to bed calmer. My life, my clock.
